title: British Grand Prix: Ferrari back on top, Antonelli heartbreak, Verstappen crashes out
author: Madeline Coleman
content:
SILVERSTONE — Charles Leclerc won a chaotic British Grand Prix Sunday for his first win since October 2024, while drivers’ championship leader Kimi Antonelli fell down the order late on as a mechanical issue struck his car towards the end of a race which finished under the safety car.

Max Verstappen was on course for a second-straight podium finish, but spun into the gravel on Lap 47 with five laps to go, bringing out the safety car.

Silverstone braced itself for one full lap of racing on the final lap, with teams being told that the safety car was ending on Lap 52, but it stayed out, leading to an anticlimactic finish.

Verstappen’s problems promoted George Russell into third. Russell then moved second after Ferrari’s decision to pit Lewis Hamilton — who looked on track for second place — cost him track position, with the seven-time champion finishing third.

It is the fourth podium of the season, and second in a row, for Russell, who did not appear to be in contention for a top-three finish for much of the race.

Antonelli was challenging for the win when he sustained a front-left wheel shield issue going over the kerb, forcing him to pit twice and leading to a five-second penalty for exceeding track limits. He finished out of the points in 16th, reducing his lead over teammate Russell at the top of the drivers’ championship to 25 points.

Madeline Coleman and Luke Smith were at Silverstone to analyze the key talking points.

Ferrari fans needed to keep their hopes and dreams in check after the start. Leclerc may have zipped past Antonelli to lead the pack, but a long 52 laps lay ahead of the grid, on a track where the long straights could expose the car’s energy deployment and power deficit.

Silverstone is an energy-starved track, featuring long straights and lacking hard braking zones where drivers can recharge their batteries. Ferrari long has said it faces a power deficit to Mercedes, but there was a sense of ‘what if’ as Leclerc continued to hold a multi-second gap over championship leader Antonelli as the race neared the halfway mark.

Leclerc hadn’t won a race since the 2024 U.S. Grand Prix, and he’s only podiumed twice this season, in Australia and Japan. Meanwhile, teammate Hamilton has thrived. The seven-time world champion secured his first victory with the team in Barcelona and three other podium finishes this season, while Leclerc has endured a rocky stint, lacking absolute confidence in qualifying.

“My driving style is quite aggressive, which seemed to work quite well at the beginning of the year,” he said, after qualifying second for Sunday’s race. “But recently, for one reason or another, it was just incredibly difficult to put things together.”

Would Sunday be different?

Leclerc pitted on Lap 26 and rejoined second, 15 seconds behind Antonelli. Mercedes opted to play the long game, and the Italian driver pushed in clean air. Leclerc was only gaining a few tenths a lap on Antonelli, a number that was dwindling as everyone waited for Antonelli to dive into the pits. The Ferrari was still just over 13 seconds behind on Lap 34.

Two laps later, Antonelli pitted and rejoined 7.7 seconds behind Leclerc. The gap was down to four seconds during the virtual safety car, and Ferrari opted against pitting Leclerc despite Antonelli having fresher tires.

It looked like Antonelli was gaining until he started slowing, diving into the pits as he reported something felt broken over the radio.

Verstappen’s crash triggered a safety car, and Ferrari opted to pit Leclerc, giving him fresh rubber. Mercedes opted to keep Russell out, putting him right on Leclerc’s tail. The race ended under a safety car, though, robbing fans of a sprint to the end.

This was the result Leclerc needed, after struggling much of this year — and it shows Ferrari has taken a step forward.

Madeline Coleman

It had all been looking so good for Antonelli. With 11 laps to go, the 19-year-old was on a charge, carving into Leclerc’s lead with fresh tires, and was poised to catch him within the next five laps.

But then it all unravelled.

“Something is broken on the car!” Antonelli cried on the radio to his race engineer, Pete Bonnington, before diving into the pits. A new front wing was fitted, but the issue persisted despite Antonelli trying his best to keep the car going. In the end, he was told to retire the car.

Antonelli kept circulating, even picking up a five-second time penalty for a track limits breach as he struggled to keep the car within the white lines due to the issue. Although he did cross the line in ninth place behind the safety car, the penalty dropped him out of the points and into 16th place.

It was a heartbreaking end to what had been such a positive weekend for Antonelli. He proved Saturday what a good groove he’d found at Silverstone, winning the sprint with some clever, tactical racing and then blasting to pole position ahead of the Ferraris.

Any hope of simply disappearing into the distance faded with Antonelli’s poor start that dropped him behind Leclerc and Hamilton, leaving him to toil in third for the opening phase of the race. By the time he picked off Hamilton, there was a four-second gap to Leclerc to try to make up.

Mercedes opted to go long on strategy, keeping Antonelli out all the way until Lap 35. It caused the gap to Leclerc to grow to almost eight seconds, yet with much fresher tires, he had the chance to put his foot down and carve into the gap, knowing the Ferrari’s Pirelli rubber was past its best.

Antonelli duly lit up the timesheets, taking three seconds out of Leclerc in two laps alone. The virtual safety car period briefly put his charge on pause, only for it to quickly resume and make the win look inevitable. And then the issue struck.

After the engine problem that cost him second place in Barcelona, it’s another difficult zero-score for Antonelli to digest as his championship lead shrinks further. Just like Barcelona, he had the measure of Russell, yet both his Mercedes teammate and Hamilton, now 32 points behind, have made healthy inroads at the top of the world championship.

A tough break for Antonelli, who can only take so much comfort from being the quickest driver Sunday.

It’s rare to see a driver of Hamilton’s prowess and experience make an error like the one at the start of the race.

But a slight misjudgement from the seven-time world champion as he waited for the five red lights to go out, creeping forward only a fraction, went down as a false start.

It didn’t stop Hamilton from making a good getaway, sweeping past Antonelli and into second place, behind Leclerc, before the first braking point at Abbey. Yet the stewards deemed his car had exceeded the allowed threshold determined by the sensors in each grid spot, triggering the penalty.

It scuppered any chance of Hamilton scoring a record-extending 10th British Grand Prix victory; the hope of which was fuelled by his sprint race pole Friday. But he didn’t seem to have the pace of either Leclerc or Antonelli, keeping the latter’s Mercedes at bay only for the first 11 laps before being overtaken.

After pitting — following a tense exchange with his race engineer about his tire life — and serving his penalty, Hamilton was left to scrap with Russell and Verstappen to recover a podium. The slow puncture for Russell and Verstappen’s decision to pit under a virtual safety car took them out of the battle, before Antonelli’s late issue moved Hamilton up to second.

Ferrari decided to pit Hamilton under the late safety car, leaving him to emerge narrowly behind the recovering Russell. But without the final-lap restart, briefly teased by race control before an updated “safety car deployed” message, Hamilton could only finish third.

A topsy-turvy race that, despite not ending in the result that Hamilton would have wanted to give his home fans, did at least end with some more Silverstone silverware and more inroads made on Antonelli at the top.

Just a week ago, optimism surrounded Red Bull after Verstappen charged to finish second in the Austrian Grand Prix, the car fitted with a significant upgrade package. He felt as if he could fight for the victory and the Dutchman said after the race it was the first time this season he felt competitive.

Silverstone, though, looked different. Red Bull’s engine clearly was struggling, as he reported issues during qualifying, and the car seemed to struggle in the high-speed corners.

Red Bull opted to not swap his engine ahead of Sunday’s race, and Verstappen looked competitive, battling with Russell early on before diving in for his first pit stop. He navigated around the Mercedes, on the outside to the Copse turn for fourth place. There was a close moment at the Stowe turn between the two, before the Red Bull pitted.

He rejoined seventh, and it became a hunt to the top. Verstappen slowly picked off his competitors, joining the fight between Hamilton and Russell. Both of them eventually pitted — but it didn’t take long for them to be on his tail. Verstappen ran third until Hamilton passed him on Lap 38, but a virtual safety car, triggered by Nico Hulkenberg, gave the Dutchman a safe pit stop, rejoining the grid fourth with fresh rubber to attack to the end.

When Antonelli began struggling with his car and fell out of podium contention, Verstappen advanced to third and looked like he was gaining on Hamilton. But it all went up in dust when the Dutchman crashed into the gravel at Stowe, ending his day and triggering a safety car.

Despite how his race ended, the questions about Red Bull’s engines likely will remain. Ferrari and Mercedes are clearly a step ahead.

Madeline Coleman
